statement: In people taking part in 572 case–control and cohort studies published from 1956 to 2012 (486,538 people with cancer; 41% of the studies from North America, 32% from Europe and 18% from Asia), drinking more than 12.5 g of ethanol a day on average (more than one drink as the review defines it) compared with not drinking (nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 24% of the studies; former drinkers were not separated) is associated with more cancers of the mouth and pharynx, the oesophagus (squamous cell carcinoma only), the larynx, the colon and rectum and the female breast, and, at heavy drinking, of the liver, with the relative risk rising with the amount (Bagnardi et al., 2015; funded by Italian cancer-research charities, no conflicts declared). The review reports no absolute risks, so its ratios cannot be turned into numbers out of 100. For heavy drinking (above 50 g a day, more than four drinks) the pooled relative risks were 5.13 (95% CI 4.31–6.10) for the mouth and pharynx, 4.95 (3.86–6.34) for oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma, 2.65 (2.19–3.19) for the larynx, 2.07 (1.66–2.58) for the liver, 1.61 (1.33–1.94) for the breast (from 11 of the 118 breast studies, editors' count) and 1.44 (1.25–1.65) for the colon and rectum; for moderate drinking (above 12.5 and up to 50 g a day) they were 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 1.08 (0.97–1.20, no clear difference), 1.23 (1.19–1.28) and 1.17 (1.11–1.24). Heavy drinking was also associated with cancers of the stomach (1.21, 1.07–1.36), pancreas (1.19, 1.11–1.28), lung (1.15, 1.02–1.30) and gallbladder (2.64, 1.62–4.30; 8 studies), and moderate drinking with small increases in prostate cancer (1.06, 1.01–1.11) and melanoma (1.20, 1.03–1.41), clear only in North American studies; there was no clear association with oesophageal adenocarcinoma or with cancers of the small intestine, cervix, endometrium, ovary, bladder or brain; and cancers of the kidney and thyroid and both kinds of lymphoma were less common in people who drank (for example non-Hodgkin's lymphoma 0.75, 0.64–0.88, at heavy drinking): for the lymphomas the authors suggest that people stop or cut down when early symptoms start, while they read the kidney result both as protection and, in their conclusion, as no association. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 study, whose own review of studies overlaps with this one, fitted risk curves that rise with intake for every cancer it included (Griswold et al., 2018). Results varied widely between studies (I² up to 91%), only 297 of the 572 studies reported adjusted estimates, so differences in smoking and other habits were often not taken into account, case–control studies gave stronger associations than cohort studies at some sites (heavy drinking and liver cancer 2.79 against 1.12; larynx 2.81 against 1.12), and the review neither appraised the studies nor tested for publication bias. That alcohol causes cancer at these sites is the judgment of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, whose list a 2021 cancer-burden model used (Rumgay et al., 2021); this pooling of observational studies cannot show it by itself. Certainty: low. Status: replicated.
plain: Across 572 studies, people who drank more than about one drink a day (12.5 g of alcohol) had more cancer of the mouth and throat, of one type of gullet cancer, of the voice box, of the bowel and of the breast than people who did not drink, and people who drank more than four drinks a day also had more liver cancer. At more than four drinks a day, mouth and throat cancer and that gullet cancer were about 5 times as common, voice-box cancer about 2.7 times, liver cancer about 2 times, breast cancer about 1.6 times and bowel cancer about 1.4 times. The review gives no numbers out of 100. Kidney and thyroid cancer and cancers of the lymph glands were less common in people who drank; for the lymph glands, the authors think this partly reflects people cutting down when they first feel ill. Results varied a lot between studies, about half the studies did not take smoking or other differences into account, and the review did not check the studies' quality. An international cancer agency judges that alcohol causes these cancers; this review alone cannot show it.
population: People in 572 case–control (409) and cohort (163) studies published 1956 to 2012 in English, 41% from North America, 32% from Europe and 18% from Asia; 486,538 people with cancer at 23 sites; ages not reported
exposure: Average alcohol intake as self-reported in each study, converted to grams of ethanol a day (one drink = 12.5 g): moderate, above 12.5 and up to 50 g a day; heavy, above 50 g a day (light drinking, up to 12.5 g, is the subject of a separate answer)
comparator: Each study's nondrinkers, combined with occasional drinkers in 138 of the 572 studies (24%); whether nondrinkers included former drinkers was not recorded
outcome: Incidence (541 studies) or death (31 studies) from cancer at 23 sites, as defined in each study
magnitude: Bagnardi et al. 2015, pooled relative risks (random effects; 95% CI) against nondrinkers or occasional drinkers, moderate then heavy drinking: mouth and pharynx 1.83 (1.62–2.07), 5.13 (4.31–6.10; I² 72%, 77%); oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma 2.23 (1.87–2.65), 4.95 (3.86–6.34; I² 85%, 91%); larynx 1.44 (1.25–1.66), 2.65 (2.19–3.19); colon and rectum 1.17 (1.11–1.24), 1.44 (1.25–1.65); liver 1.08 (0.97–1.20), 2.07 (1.66–2.58); female breast 1.23 (1.19–1.28), 1.61 (1.33–1.94; I² 54%, 10%; heavy from 11 studies, editors' count); heavy only: stomach 1.21 (1.07–1.36), pancreas 1.19 (1.11–1.28), lung 1.15 (1.02–1.30), gallbladder 2.64 (1.62–4.30); moderate: prostate 1.06 (1.01–1.11), melanoma 1.20 (1.03–1.41); inverse: kidney moderate 0.79 (0.72–0.86), thyroid moderate 0.81 (0.71–0.94), Hodgkin's lymphoma heavy 0.63 (0.41–0.97), non-Hodgkin's lymphoma heavy 0.75 (0.64–0.88). By design, heavy drinking: mouth and pharynx 5.34 (4.46–6.39; 35 case–control studies) against 3.13 (1.59–6.19; 3 cohort studies); liver 2.79 (2.00–3.87; 24 case–control) against 1.12 (1.02–1.23; 7 cohort); larynx 2.81 (2.33–3.39) against 1.12 (0.75–1.67; 3 cohort). No absolute risks reported.

risk_of_bias.note: Bagnardi et al. (card sc_bagnardi_2015: AMSTAR 2 critically low): no protocol, no appraisal of the primary studies, and adjusted estimates pooled with crude ones (297 of 572 studies adjusted); case–control studies, open to recall and control-selection bias, are 409 of the 572 and gave stronger associations than cohorts at several sites; residual confounding by smoking is possible for the mouth, pharynx, oesophagus, larynx, lung and stomach. Counted once.

inconsistency.note: I² reaches 91% at heavy drinking, so the size differs widely between studies, but for the main sites the direction is the same across designs, sexes and world regions (Tables 2 to 4), and the claim gives design-specific figures rather than one number; not rated down.

indirectness.note: Self-reported average intake and cancer incidence (541 studies) or death (31) in the populations studied, as the claim says; drinking pattern and beverage type were not analysed and the claim does not speak to them.

imprecision.note: Narrow intervals for the moderate and heavy estimates at the main sites; the liver estimate at moderate intake includes 1 and is reported as no clear difference; the gallbladder estimate rests on 8 studies.

publication_bias.note: Not examined in this review (the authors refer to their earlier site-specific reviews); small-study effects could inflate the moderate-intake estimates but are unlikely to produce relative risks of 2 to 5; stated, not rated down.

large_effect.note: Relative risks near 5 for the mouth, pharynx and oesophagus at heavy drinking, but confounding by smoking, a bias away from the null, remains in many estimates, and the cohort estimate for the mouth and pharynx is 3.13 (1.59–6.19; 3 cohorts); not applied.

dose_response.note: At each main site the relative risk rises from light to moderate to heavy drinking, and the dose–response meta-regression, which allows for correlation within studies, shows steep rises for the mouth, pharynx and oesophageal squamous cell carcinoma (Figure 3); part of the category gradient compares different sets of studies.

grade.reasoning: Observational evidence starts low; it is rated down one level for risk of bias and up one level for the dose–response gradient, which gives low; a strict reading without the upgrade would give very low. Rated as worded: an association that grows with the amount; that alcohol causes these cancers is the classification of the International Agency for Research on Cancer, cited by the papers, and is not tested by this pooling. The Global Burden of Disease 2016 review shares many primary studies with this one, and the 2021 model only uses IARC's list, so neither is counted as independent replication. Status replicated: independent subsets of the 572 studies, by design, sex and world region, agree in direction for the main sites.
